## Results {#sec-results}

<!-- Describe the results that you received from the methods described earlier. -->

This section presents the substantive findings from the retained models identified in @sec-modeling. The aim is no longer to compare candidate specifications, but to interpret what the retained models suggest about chess behavior and structure across the main domains of the project: metagame dynamics, opening popularity, time use, player progression, and player categorization.

Accordingly, the section emphasizes interpretable summaries of model output, including estimated effects, representative predicted values, and descriptive profile summaries where appropriate. Inferential claims are drawn only from models retained for that purpose, while descriptive models are used more cautiously to summarize structure and variation in the data. Each subsection therefore focuses on what the retained model or models show, how large the relevant patterns are, and how confidently those patterns can be described.

### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics-3}

The intent of metagame-dynamics models was to characterize the state and evolution of the metagame across time and format. The model category accomplishes this on two levels. Aggregate metagame metrics (macro models) operate at the ecosystem level, while opening composition models help contextualize those aggregate shifts by clarifying what kinds of opening-level substitutions accompany them. The clearest changes concern concentration and diversity, while broader game-environment outcomes changed less consistently.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{tc,t}
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1 t
+
\beta_2 \,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3 \,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4 \, t \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5 \, t \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_{tc,t}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained macro metagame model. Here, $Y_{tc,t}$ denotes a month-by-time-control metagame outcome, such as HHI concentration, effective number of openings, draw rate, upset rate, or average moves. Inference used Newey--West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-macro}
\end{figure}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_t = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{k,t})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{j,t})}, \\
\eta_{k,t}
&=
\alpha_k + \beta_k t,
\qquad k=1,\dots,K.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained multinomial metagame-composition model, fit separately by time control. Here, $Y_t$ denotes the opening category at month $t$, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-multinomial}
\end{figure}
```


Across formats, opening usage became less concentrated and more diverse (see table \ref{tab:metagame-macro-estimates}). This trend is present for all three time controls, though its magnitude differs. HHI fell over time in the baseline format (blitz), with an estimate of $-2.283 \times 10^{-6}, \ p = 0.002$; this trend was more pronounced in rapid ($-7.440 \times 10^{-6}, \ p < 0.001$) and classical ($-1.694 \times 10^{-5}, \ p = 0.022$). The number of effective openings ($N_\text{eff}$) rose over time in the baseline format, with an estimate of $0.1021, \ p = 0.002$; this trend was also more pronounced in rapid ($0.2411, \ p < 0.001$) and classical ($0.5556, \ p = 0.030$). These trends move in opposite-yet-complementary directions, as declining concentration and increasing diversity are expressing the same core pattern. Overall, the time-control interactions matter substantively, not just statistically.

```{r Metagame Results Figure}
#| label: fig-metagame-results
#| fig-cap: "Predicted model values over time."
#| fig-align: center

p_macro_fit <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_macro_fit.rds")
p_macro_fit
```

Also present in table \ref{tab:metagame-macro-estimates} are outcomes. Draw rate and and average moves present little evidence of a systematic linear trend, the lowest p-value among their estimates being 0.215 for the baseline time trend. Upset rate shows some evidence of a positive baseline time trend ($9.540 \times 10^{-5}, \ p = 0.024$), but it's weak and not clearly generalized across formats; the non-baseline trends for upset rate have p-values more in line with draw rate and average moves. This is important, as it means that ecosystem structure changed more clearly than these broader, game-environment outcomes did.

Whereas the aggregate metrics show that the metagame broadened, the composition model provides a way to describe which opening-share shifts underlie the aggregate broadening of the metagame. The compositional patterns were estimated separately by time control, allowing format-specific movement to be compared. Of note is that the composition findings are based on models with comparable performance across formats; table \ref{tab:metagame-composition-model-comparison} shows blitz, rapid, and classical to have held-out errors of 0.910, 0.923, and 0.940, respectively.

The observed macro diversification reflects broad redistribution across the opening ecosystem rather than a single new opening taking over, and the compositional results reflect that: From table \ref{tab:metagame-multinomial-robustness}, "Other" is the top increase at every $k$, and a named opening decline remains visible once the retained opening set is sufficiently rich. The pattern is stable enough to suggest ecosystem-wide redistribution, as if "Other" gains share constantly, it means that the metagame isn't just rotating among a fixed set of dominant openings. Instead, some of the change is occurring outside the most explicitly-retained openings, which is consistent with diversification.

<!-- Potentially move held-out errors into a new paragraph here and add additional format-specific mover output (additional model stuff) later. -->

The claim of broad redistribution is not merely a modeling artifact of a single cutoff. Table \ref{tab:metagame-multinomial-robustness} shows that "Other" remains the top increase, and the top negative mover stabilizes as French Defense: Knight Variation at $k = 12$ and $k = 16$. While log loss increases from 0.674 at $k = 8$ to 0.910 at $k = 12$ to 1.127 at $k = 16$, this is reflective of increasing $k$ making the prediction mechanically more difficult; the broad directional composition remains stable, even if log loss increases with $k$.

All in all, at the ecosystem level, the metagame became less concentrated and more diverse over time, and those structural changes differed in severity across time controls. The opening-level evidence suggests that this broadening reflects diffuse substitution within the opening ecosystem rather than one simple adoption cycle. The clearest evidence concerns ecosystem structure, and not parallel shifts in draw rate or average moves.

### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity-3}

The goal of the opening-popularity category of models is simple, because they're really just asking what factors impact opening choice. The retained pooled multinomial model was used so summarize opening popularity as a compositional outcome. This is a very similar approach to the opening-level method applied in @sec-metagame-dynamics-3, the difference being that the prior section was concerned only about explaining and supporting metagame-level drift, whereas this one explores opening choice in much more depth.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_i = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{ik})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{ij})}, \\
\eta_{ik}
&=
\alpha_k
+
\beta_{1k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i
+
\beta_{2k}\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_{3k}\,t_i
+
\beta_{4k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i
\cdot
\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained pooled multinomial opening-popularity model. Here, $Y_i$ denotes the opening category for month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin cell $i$, $t_i$ is the month index, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories, including "Other".}
\label{fig:eq-opening-popularity}
\end{figure}
```


Opening popularity is not random across skill levels or formats. This is best evidenced by table \ref{tab:opening-popularity-rating-profile}. As it's an aggregate, the residual "Other" category will almost always be dominant when modeling with a top-$k$ approach (for any reasonable $k$) simply due to the sheer quantity of named openings that see play at every level. Of greater importance are the share of the Other category, the share and presence of the top non-Other openings, and how those numbers change across skill and time control. Among explicitly-modeled openings, lower-rated bins show more mass on openings like the Philidor Defense, Scandinavian Defense, and Queen's Pawn Game, while higher-rated bins shift toward the Caro-Kann Defense and the Accelerated London System^[While the London System technically falls under the umbrella of the Queen's Pawn Game – they begin very similarly – it's often considered to be distinct from the more typical set of Queen's Pawn openings, which is why I'm using it as an example of a shift in opening popularity.] This supports the claim that opening popularity varies systematically by skill level, and that the pattern is visible across time controls.

In both blitz and rapid, the dominant Other category grows with rating, from 0.732/0.768 at an 800 rating, 0.835/0.840 at 1600, and 0.892/0.877 at 2400 for blitz/rapid, respectively. This implies that higher-rated players place more of their opening mass outside the named top openings retained in the model. A rating pattern also presents itself where specific openings are concerned: For both blitz and rapid, the Philidor Defense is popular at 800, the Queen's Pawn Game is popular at 1600, and the Caro-Kann defense is popular at 2400. The identity and order of the top named openings is not identical, however, suggesting that time control shapes popularity within rating strata, even when the broader rating gradient is similar.

```{r Opening-Popularity Results Figure}
#| label: fig-opening-popularity-results
#| fig-cap: "Predicted share for choice openings."
#| fig-align: center

p_opening_rating <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_opening_rating.rds")
p_opening_rating
```

Changes in opening popularity over time are present, but modest in magnitude. As seen in table \ref{tab:opening-popularity-time-change} and elaborated on in @sec-metagame-dynamics-3, the time trend is directionally consistent across formats, the slight positive trend for Other pointing to broad compositional shifts rather than a dramatic takeover by one opening. In both formats, the largest named positive mover is the Accelerated London System, and the largest named negative mover is the French Defense: Knight Variation.

The popularity results are based on the retained pooled multinomial model, which showed reasonable held-out performance on the test set with a log loss of 0.893 (see table \ref{tab:opening-popularity-model-comparison}). The one-opening models provide supporting checks, but the multinomial is the relevant basis for interpreting substitution across openings. Table \ref{tab:opening-popularity-robustness} tested linear and spline fits for both rating and time, as well as different top-$k$ thresholds. Allowing nonlinear rating slightly improved fit (log loss of 0.890 compared to 0.893), whereas allowing nonlinear time slightly worsened fit (0.895 compared to 0.893), though the improvements were incredibly marginal; the simpler linear-time specification is adequate for baseline reporting. As addressed in @sec-metagame-dynamics, an increase in $k$ saw a corresponding increase in log loss (0.666 for $k = 8$ up to 1.111 for $k = 16$), but this increase in modeling difficulty does not overturn the broad pattern of modest, consistent changes. As such, these conclusions don't appear to depend heavily on one narrow functional-form choice.

Ultimately, these models found that opening popularity varies systematically by rating and time control. Higher-rated bins allocate more share outside the explicitly-retained top openings. Over time, the largest changes are modest but directionally consistent across blitz and rapid. The most visible temporal change is a rise in the residual other category alongside smaller named increases and decreases.

### Time Use {#sec-time-use-3}
<!-- I do not yet have coefficients/model estimates, so currently have some placeholders -->

This category of models characterizes how players allocate time and experience time pressure across rating and time control; time use is being treated as a behavioral outcome that may vary by skill and the structure of the format. Two different models were retained for this category: interaction-based mean models for average time use, and a fractional quasibinomial model for low-time frequency. Average time use was modeled separately at the macro and player-month levels, but the results found in this section are taken from the player-level interaction model. Across the retained models, the clearest time-use pattern is a format-specific rating gradient: Stronger players use less time on average in blitz, but more in rapid and especially classical, implying that the relationship between skill and time allocation changes direction across formats. Low-time frequency was found to increase with rating in all formats, especially blitz.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AvgTime}_i
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{Rating}_i \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{Rating}_i \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained player-level mean time-use model. Here, $\mathrm{AvgTime}_i$ denotes average time spent for observation $i$, and the interaction terms allow the rating slope to vary by time control.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-mean}
\end{figure}
```

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}\!\left(\mathbb{E}[L_i \mid X_i]\right)
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained fractional low-time model. Here, $L_i \in [0,1]$ denotes low-time frequency for observation $i$.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-lowtime}
\end{figure}
```


Per table \ref{tab:timeuse-mean-model-comparison} interaction specifications were retained at both levels due to slightly superior WRMSE (0.143 vs. 0.149 for macro and 1.832 vs. 1.839 for player-month). Though it's a marginal improvement, it implies that a common rating effect across time controls was slightly inadequate. Therefore, the substantive results should be interpreted in terms of format-specific rating relationships rather than one universal rating slope. As shown in the format difference are much substantial when taking model estimates into account, with blitz at the lowest (4.390 seconds per move at 800, 3.834 at 1600, and 3.279 at 2400), classical at the highest (800: 10.573, 1600: 12.396, 2400: 14.220), and rapid somewhere in between (800: 6.448, 1600: 7.136, 2400: 7.824). Notably, blitz is the only of the three with a negative rating gradient, and classical presents a much wider confidence interval, suggesting greater uncertainty (see table \ref{tab:timeuse-player-mean-profile}).

Though no relevant tables are present for the sake of brevity, it should be noted that interaction specifications were retained for the mean models because a common rating slope was inadequate. The negative baseline rating effect for blitz and positive rapid interaction were directionally consistent across supporting models. The classical interaction, however, was less stable and should therefore be interpreted more cautiously.

On the whole, time-use behavior varies strongly across both rating and format. The relationship between rating and average time-use is format-specific, whereas low-time frequency rises with rating in all formats. Faster formats produce substantially more time pressure overall, which is expected. Therefore, average pace and acute time pressure should be treated as related-yet-distinct aspects of player behavior.

### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression-3}

The retained player fixed-effects models are being used to assess whether within-player changes in current-month behavior are associated with later rating movement, and if so, which behaviors are associated with what kinds of change (i.e., rating gain/loss). Three targets were retained: 1-month rating change, 3-month change, and absolute 1-month change. The signed (non-absolute) targets ask whether a predictor relates to a player moving up or down in rating, with positive values reflecting positive increases and vice versa. In contrast, the absolute target removes direction, and asks whether a predictor relates to moving more or less, regardless of direction—  positive values reflect larger changes, while negative ones imply smaller ones. 

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{it}^{(h)}
&=
\alpha_i
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{AvgRating}_{it}
+
\beta_2\,\mathrm{Games}_{it}
+
\beta_3\,\mathrm{AvgMoves}_{it} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{OpeningDiversity}_{it}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{TopOpeningShare}_{it}
+
\beta_6\,\mathrm{SwitchedOpening}_{it}
+
\varepsilon_{it},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Generic form of the retained player fixed-effects progression model, where $Y_{it}^{(h)} \in \{\Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+1}, \Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+3}, |\Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+1}|\}$.}
\label{fig:eq-progression-fe-generic}
\end{figure}
```

Table \ref{tab:progression-fe-results} shows that, for signed targets, higher current rating is associated with more negative subsequent rating change. Conversely, average moves, opening diversity, and switching one's most-played opening are positively associated with rating signed rating change. For the absolute-change target, average moves, opening diversity, and opening switching are all negatively associated with month-to-month volatility.

This is particularly relevant when it comes to favorable (positive) signed predictors, as it means that every favorable predictor is associated with less absolute movement.

Table \ref{tab:progression-fe-contrasts} helps convert the fixed-effect estimates into practical differences across representative predictor values. It compares continuous predictors are compared at the 25th and 75th percentiles, while the switching indicator is compared from 0 to 1. All magnitude patterns are directionally consistent with the coefficient table. Moving from lower to higher values of average moves corresponds to a meaningful increase in signed rating change. To a degree, this is also true of opening diversity, with the only difference being its modest range at the 3-month target compared to its 1-month counterpart (decreases from [6.052, 8.816] to [0.915, 4.852]). Switching the most-played opening is a smaller but still impactful contrast. All three are associated with smaller absolute movement. 

Of particular note is current average rating, as its signed intervals are orders of magnitude larger than any of the other predictors. This does not imply that its importance as a predictor is equally large, however; rather, it's on a very wide scale, which impacts the size of the interval. As an example, for 1-month change, the 25th percentile rating is ~1272, while the 75th is ~1798, for a difference of ~526 rating points. Multiply that by the coefficient of -0.469 and you get a contrast near $-0.469 \times 526 \approx -247$. Compare this to average moves, where the 25th–75th gap is only about 7 moves, opening diversity where it's ~46 units, or top-opening share, where it's less than 0.1, and you'll see why the contrast band for average rating is so much larger.

Not all retained predictors show equally clear evidence; games played and top-opening share stand out for being weak or ambiguous predictors. Refer back to table \ref{tab:progression-fe-results}. Neither have a p-value below 0.1 for any of the targets, and most are many times that. Their poor evaluation is further reinforced by table \ref{tab:progression-fe-contrasts}, as still neither have a confidence interval that precludes zero. Current average rating is of note for being the only predictor whose statistical significance crosses a meaningful alpha of 0.05 between models, with a p-value of 0.959 for the absolute target. This is expected, however, and actually a good sign that the models are on the right track. The Lichess rating system is designed so that a player's current rating is already a good summary of expected strength, so we actually shouldn't expect that it should predict larger or smaller absolute next-month movement; it would be more worrying if the coefficient weren't centered near 0.

It's important to remember that the fixed-effect design isolates within-player association; these targets are being modeled as within-player associations, not as cross-sectional differences between players. The models are estimated on large within-player panels in order to support stable coefficient estimation. Note that the signed-change models explain substantially more within-player variation than the absolute-change model – within-$R^2$ values of 0.270, 0.453, and 0.004 for 1-month, 3-month, and 1-month absolute, respectively – so the latter is best treated as a supporting magnitude benchmark rather than the main target.

Within players, months characterized by higher move-count games, broader opening diversity, and switching one's most-played opening are associated with more favorable next-month rating movement. Those same predictors are not associated with larger movement magnitude in the absolute model, but are instead most often associated with smaller absolute change. By contrast, games played and top-opening share do not show comparably stable evidence in the retained fixed-effects specification. These results suggest that the behavioral signals most associated with later progression concern game complexity, repertoire breadth, and active repertoire adjustment rather than simple activity volume or repertoire concentration alone.

### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization-3}

Though it has been mentioned multiple times in @sec-player-categorization-2, it is important to stress that no player-categorization model is fit for inference; even the retained $k$-means solution should only be treated as a descriptive summary of behavioral variation across player-month observations. The point here is not to treat the clusters as latent causal types, but to describe recurring patterns in performance, repertoire structure, and activity. The results below use standardized cluster centers, time-control distributions, and month-to-month persistence summaries.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\min_{C_1,\dots,C_6}
\sum_{k=1}^{6}
\sum_{i \in C_k}
\left\| x_i - \mu_k \right\|^2,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained $k$-means clustering objective for player categorization. Here, $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ denotes the standardized feature vector for observation $i$, $C_k$ denotes cluster $k$, and $\mu_k$ denotes the centroid of cluster $k$.}
\label{fig:eq-categorization-kmeans}
\end{figure}
```


As described in tables \ref{tab:categorization-standardized-performance} and \ref{tab:categorization-standardized-repertoire}, clusters differ along multiple axes rather than only average rating. Clusters 1 and 2 are foils: the former contains wide-repertoire, high-activity, and above-average-rated players, whereas the latter has lower-rated, lower-activity, narrow-repertoire players whose games are shorter on average. Cluster 3 is notable for very high opening switching and somewhat lower opening concentration, but is otherwise close to the sample center. Clusters 4 and 5 both contain strong players, but are behaviorally distinct, with cluster 4 grouping players with longer games and high draw rates, and cluster 5 grouping players with high win rates and positive rating differentials. Finally, cluster 6 prefers players with concentrated openings, low switching, and moderate activity. In general, the clusters are especially concerned with diversity, concentration, switching, and game structure.

Though unsuitable for inference, the retained $k$-means categorization solution is useful because it captures multiple distinct dimensions of behavior, those profiles are unevenly distributed across format, and that they show only moderate persistence over time. They do not, however, establish sharply-separated latent types or imply stable archetypes. At the end of the day, the clustering solution serves as a descriptive map of player-month behavior, but its moderate persistence and uneven transition structure suggest that these clusters are better understood as recurring behavioral profiles than anything more concrete.

## Discussion

<!--

### Principal Findings {#sec-discussion}

The retained models collectively point to structured variation in online chess behavior across both ecosystem-level and player-level domains. The metagame became less concentrated and more diverse; opening choice varied systematically by rating and time control; time use reflected multiple behavioral dimensions rather than one simple skill gradient; progression was associated more with complexity, breadth, and adaptation; and player categorization identified recurring behavioral profiles as opposed to fixed player types. The main interpretive question, then, is not whether structure exists, but what the structure suggests about metagame change, player decision-making, and behavioral development.

One of the most consistent patterns present in the results is that they repeatedly argue against simple, one-dimensional explanations: metagame change was not just a story of one opening taking over, time management was not reducible to one general measure of efficiency, and progression was not best explained by activity volume alone. Instead, the findings point toward more diverse outcomes. Diversification is interesting because a simple prior expectation might have been convergence around a smaller number of dominant openings or strategies; it suggests that greater access to theory, engines, and content may be expanding participation in the opening space rather than narrowing it, and implies that player development may benefit more from experimentation and differentiation than optimization towards one best repertoire.

The subsections that follow interpret these findings in greater depth, focusing on what they imply about metagame evolution, opening choice, time-management behavior, progression, and the meaning of the retained behavioral profiles.^[Though no prior expectations were formally established at this project's outset, the subsections may sometimes draw comparisons between the results and hypothetical expectations which might otherwise have been made.]

### Metagame Structure and Opening Choice {#sec-metagame-and-opening-discussion}

<!-- 
Include citation for metagames converging, maybe?
-->

The strongest ecosystem-level finding was the paired decline in concentration and rise in effective diversity across time controls; the metagame broadened over time. This is meaningful because metagames are convergent in nature; they seek to optimize gameplay to its logical extreme, which is an inherently reductive process. While the results cannot support an inferential claim about whether the increase in diversity is a result of an online chess environment compared to chess itself, it isn't implausible to speculate that the massive quantity of diverse people playing online chess may be fostering diversification by pushing back against a strategic collapse toward a few dominant lines. Also of note is the game's immense mathematical complexity, which necessarily makes convergence to an optimal strategy more difficult.

On the opening-choice front, the clearest structure in opening popularity came from rating and format rather than over-time drift. The results found that opening choice was deeply stratified by player strength, with time control modifying the player-strength structure instead of replacing it. Temporal changes are directionally consistent across formats, but modest in magnitude. The opening metagame therefore looks like a layered system of skill-stratified preferences plus moderate temporal drift.

Important is the distinction between diversification as a measure of which openings are most popular and diversification as a measure of total opening share. The former implies that the top openings simply shuffled around, cyclically taking each other's place over time, while the latter implies that the share of the Other category of openings actually increases over time. This dichotomy is important because metagames often move in cyclical patterns, best illustrated by the game of rock-paper-scissors.

Suppose that chess openings can be likened to rock-paper-scissors, where any given opening can map to one of the three options— rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. Now suppose that 50% of chess players favor openings which map to rock, while scissors and paper are each only favored by 25% of players. Assuming completely random matchmaking, scissors-style openings become disproportionately likely to lose, and paper-style openings become conversely likely to win. Canny players will recognize this dynamic, and begin to play paper at a higher rate. Let's say 15% of all scissors players switch to paper. Now, scissors has the disproportionate advantage. That is, until rock players catch on and swap to paper and the cycle repeats itself. In a perfect world, the metagame would converge to a point where each type had an opening share of $1/3$, but in practice, metagames tend to remain cyclical.

Now, it isn't actually reasonable to map chess openings to a rock-paper-scissors structure, but that's not the point of the hypothetical. The point is that even after converging to a point where rock, paper, and scissors each have an equal opening share, there are still only three options in use; if the top openings shift around, but the quantity of unique openings played remains the same, then all that's really happened is a shift among the most popular openings. The opening diversification supported by the results contrast such an eventuality by showing that the Other category of openings is actually increasing in share over time, which suggests that the Lichess playerbase is expanding in breadth.

Overall, these findings complicate at least two simple expectations: First, more theory and shared content might have led to convergence, and second, metagame change might have been expected to appear mostly as visible named-opening turnover. Instead, the results suggest broad diversification, long-tail expansion, and strong rating structuring.

### Time Management as Multi-Dimensional Behavior {#sec-time-discussion}

Average time use and low-time frequency are related, but not interchangeable. In blitz, stronger players use less time on average and low-time frequency increases with rating. In rapid and classical, stronger players use more time on average, but low-time frequency also increases rating. As such, the time-use results suggest that time management has at least two distinct components that shouldn't be treated as a single skill gradient: baseline pacing, and exposure to acute time pressure.

The rating gradient in average time changes sign by format. In other words, using more time does not have the same behavioral meaning in all time controls. In blitz, stronger players may be able to play faster on average because of better pattern recognition, more stable repertoires, or stronger intuition. In slower formats, stronger players may instead choose to invest more time because the format allows deeper calculation and more deliberate planning. With that in mind, faster average play in blitz should not automatically be read as lower engagement or lower complexity, and slower average play in rapid/classical should not automatically be read as 'better' time management in a universal sense.

Low-time frequency rises with rating in all formats. This argues against a plausible prior expectation equating skill with uniformly safer or smoother time use. Instead, stronger players may think more deeply in critical moments, play sharper or more demanding positions, or tolerate more pressure because of greater confidence or comfort. It's reasonable to speculate that, rather than simply playing 'faster' or 'slower' according to the time control, skilled players are more active and selective in how they allocate time, accepting future pressure in exchange for better decisions in critical positions.

### Progression, Adaptation, and Player Development {#sec-player-progression-discussion}

The simplest assumption to make pertaining to improvement in any skill is that improvement is driven primarily by time spent practicing said skill. In the context of chess data, a reasonable prior expectation might be that player activity is the salient predictor of player growth. The results, however, found otherwise; the retained models liked more favorable later-rating movement to higher average moves, greater opening diversity, and switching the most-played opening. In contrast, games played was weak and inconclusive, suggesting that improvement is associated more with how players engage with the game than to how much they play.

Broadening repertoires and changing the most-played opening are behaviors consistent with an adaptive, flexible style, which is meaningful because fixed, narrow repetition is often assumed to be the cleaner developmental path. The results suggest otherwise, supporting the notion that repertoire adjustment and breadth may coincide with favorable rating movement. Ergo, development involve strategic exploration as well as consolidation.

The absolute-change model helps clarify the signed-change results, though due to a low within-$R^2$, it's best read as a supporting benchmark. None of the favorable signed predictors were associated with greater movement magnitude; all had negative coefficients for the absolute-change model. This has interesting implications. For one, it weakens the argument that the strong results for experimentatative behavior is merely a consequence of experimentation's high-variance nature. More importantly, however, it implies that none of the positive-leaning predictors has an extreme or immediate impact on next-month rating. In effect, while the results support experimental play as a potential indicator of further improvement, they failed to find predictors for 'overnight improvement', instead modeling the improvement process as a gradual change occurring over time; there doesn't seem to be 'one quick trick to instantly improve your rating by 100 points'.

To be clear, the progression results are less a claim that playing more does not matter than a claim that raw volume has limited additional explanatory value once game complexity, repertoire breadth, and repertoire adjustment are taken into account. In that sense, the retained models suggest diminishing returns to volume alone and a comparatively stronger role for adaptive engagement. 

Overall, the progression results favor a development story centered on adaptation and complexity, which contrasts with a simpler 'play more and optimize more' account. @sec-metagame-dynamics-3 and @sec-metagame-and-opening-discussion make this pattern plausible, since the ecosystem itself is diverse and players appear to move among behavioral configurations. Improvement may therefore be best understood as an adaptive process rather than a purely accumulative one. 

### Behavioral Profiles as Descriptive States {#sec-categorization-discussion}

The clustering models are in somewhat of a tricky spot, because even though they were largely successful, they're unfit for inference. As such, this section makes no attempts to provide conclusive or inferential claims, and instead intends to ask what it means for the clustering to have succeeded and the potential implications of that success.

The retained clustering solution differentiates player-month among multiple behavioral axes: skill, repertoire breadth, opening switching, game length and draw structure, and activity. For example, cluster 1 contains high-diversity, high-activity, and above-average-rated players, while cluster 2 contrasts this with, with lower-rated, low-activity, narrower-repertoire players. This is salient because it means the model isn't simply reproducing the Lichess skill ranking, and instead identifies distinct configurations of chess behavior.

Were the clusters sharply stable, they might look like enduring player types, but because persistence is moderate and transitions between clusters are common, they're better interpreted as recurring behavioral states or configurations. This descriptive-state reading is consistent with the rest of the results: A broadening opening ecosystem and adaptive progression patterns both suggest behavioral movement, so the clusters may therefore reflect temporary strategic priorities, developmental phases, or context-dependent styles. This makes them useful as summaries of behavior, but not as definitive labels of what a player 'is'.

Ultimately, although the retained clustering solution is not itself inferential, its success suggest that player behavior is structured enough to motivate more explicit state-based analyses in future work. Because the clusters are both interpretable and fluid, a natural next step would be to model transitions among behavioral profiles directly and ask how those movements relate to development, format, or repertoire change. In short, the fact that the models work so well at classifying player behavior is more important than any of their descriptive interpretations.

### Practical Uses and Broader Implications {#sec-implications-discussion}

The models presented here provide a general framework for studying chess behavior across multiple levels. Those levels include metagame structure, opening choice, time-use behavior, player progression, and descriptive behavioral profiling. Because each level showed interpretable structure, the framework appears reusable beyond the bounds of this paper and its accompanying dataset. Future work could apply the same framework to platform comparisons, longer time periods, or more explicit transition modeling.

The results also point toward potential practical uses for coaching and training contexts. The progression models imply that richer and more adaptive engagement may be more informative than game volume alone. The time-use models imply that average pace and low-time pressure should be treated as separate aspects of player behavior. Together, this suggests that player-facing tools could offer more useful diagnostics by tracking breadth and adjustment rather than only game counts or raw performance outcomes.

Beyond direct practical use, the results suggest a broader method of understanding chess behavior, indicating that the multiple behavioral levels modeled are interconnected pieces of a greater whole as opposed to unrelated outcomes. This is important because these domains are often studied independently. The broader value of the retained models is therefore not just that they fit these data, but that they help organize chess-behavior research as a multi-level system.

### Limitations {#sec-limitations-discussion}

The retained model results are laboring under several limitations, two of which are all-encompassing. First, this entire project is observational in nature, and thus cannot make strong causal claims. All inference presented in this work is therefore limited to associations between variables rather than claims that one directly influences the other. For example, opening diversity and switching are associated with rating increase, but the models do not prove that increasing diversity or switching causes improvement; similarly, time-use patterns should not be read as causal mechanisms of strength and instead as correlated behavioral signatures. Even the fixed-effects models, while stronger than purely cross-sectional comparisons, still do not eliminate all time-varying confounding. This is the project's most important limitation: That all retained results are derived from observational data, so even the strongest inferential findings must be interpreted as such.

Second, the data gathered for the project was intentionally limited in size and scope— size for reproducibility purposes, and scope because the project set out to explore several facets of online chess behavior. In a more focused study, the modeling process would have access to a dataset tailored to the project's specific goals (e.g., the inclusion of move data to better model individual games). Greater specificity can also indirectly afford larger datasets, as those built to accommodate multiple different modeling goals effectively 'waste' space by including fields that aren't necessary for all research questions. Admittedly, this is not a limitation of the core modeling framework so much as a consequence of the format this project was built upon and the concern for reproducibility therein, but the reason for a limitations existence does not obviate its effect.

Also related to the scope and scale of the data is granularity. The game of chess is an unfathomably-complex strategic space, to the point that it's functionally impossible to model in full detail; there is simply not a computer on the planet that could even get close to accomplishing such a task. To that end, each model necessarily compresses a much richer behavioral space into something capable of being modeled. Part of this compression happened during the parsing pipeline (see @sec-source), but some models took additional steps to further simplify the data. For instance, the top-$k$ opening models rely on a large residual Other category, which is substantively meaningful but still aggregates many heterogeneous openings; some retained models depend on linear or otherwise simple functional forms; and some estimates, especially in slower formats or sparse settings, are less stable or more uncertain.

Finally, it must be acknowledged that the data used for modeling are both relative to a specific platform in Lichess and dependent on the time period studied. The results should accordingly not be used to describe online chess behavior as a whole, but interpreted in the context of the Lichess population from January 2024 through December 2025. It might be that other platforms like Chess.com show similar results or that the Lichess ecosystem behaved very similarly in years prior to 2024, but it's equally possible that those alternate populations behave in entirely different manners.

<!--
\newpage
-->

### Furture Work {#sec-future-work}

The clearest and most immediate next step is to apply the retained modeling framework to richer and more-targeted datasets that allow greater depth within each substantive domain. This project was intentionally broad and reproducible, which made it possible to study several facets of online chess behaviors at once, but limited how deeply any one domain could be modeled. Future work could accordingly trade breadth for depth by using larger and more specialized datasets to model particular questions with greater specificity. Potential avenues include move-level game data, richer opening annotations, and more detailed and longer-spanning player histories.

The current results also point to several specific questions that deserve more direct study. Included among such questions are: whether metagame broadening reflects experimentation or mere long-tail expansion; whether low-time frequency among stronger players reflects sharper positions or more selective time investment; and whether repertoire adjustment is a genuine precursor to improvement or simply a correlate of broader behavioral change. Follow-up studies could test these mechanisms more directly by building models around the unresolved processes suggested by our results rather than only refining the same descriptive summaries.

A final priority for future work is to evaluate the external generality of the present findings. Our results are tied to Lichess and to a specific time window, making cross-platform and cross-period comparison especially important. Replication on other platforms or different time periods would help identify which patterns are platform-specific and which are more general features of online chess. If the framework proves stable across settings, it could support broader comparative chess research with possible wide-ranging implications.
